questions.problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(0,1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}={2}^{x+y}y(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+1)$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P(0,1,0)$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(0,1).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1) & ={2}^{0+1}(1)(0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2)+1)=2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,2,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}={x}^{2}y+2x-y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(-2,2,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(-2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,2) & =(-2)^{2}(2)+2(-2)-(2) \\  & =8-4-2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-2,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,2)}(y-2) \\ z-1 & =2(y-2) \\ z & =2y-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,2,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=2y-3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=5.$ Given that the point $P(4,5,-2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\frac{\sqrt{{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}}}{2x-y}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=5.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(4,5).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(4,5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(4,5) & =\frac{\sqrt{(5)^{2}-(4)^{2}}}{2(4)-(5)} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{9}}{3} \\  & =\frac{3}{3} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(4,5) & ={f}_{x}(4,5)(x-4) \\ z-(-2) & =1(x-4) \\ z+2 & =x-4 \\ z & =x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,5,-2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y=5 \\ z=x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=5,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-6$ (or $x-z-6=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $-i-k$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-(-i-k)=i+k$ is also parallel to it.

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=3\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)-(x+y)^{3}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =3\operatorname{ln}⁡(0+1)-(1+0)^{3} \\  & =3\cdot 0-{1}^{3} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =-1(y) \\ z+1 & =-y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$

questions.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=e.$ Given that the point $P(e,2,3)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-\frac{{e}^{y}}{{x}^{2}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=e.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(e,2,3)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(e,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(e,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(e,2) & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\frac{{e}^{2}}{{e}^{2}} \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(e,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(e,2)}(y-2) \\ z-3 & =1(y-2) \\ z & =y+1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(e,2,3)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=e \\ z=y+1\end{aligned}
$$
